mechanism: U.S. importers pay a 50 percent tariff on Canadian wine, which raises the landed cost and reduces order volumes from U.S. buyers.
U.S. buyers shift from tariffed Canadian wine to domestically produced wine, lifting domestic producer sales.
U.S. importers pay the 50 percent tariff on Canadian cement, making Canadian supply less competitive against domestic and other sources.
Tariffs on Canadian cement raise input costs for U.S. construction projects that had sourced Canadian cement.
U.S. buyers pay the 50 percent tariff on Canadian honey, reducing its price competitiveness in U.S. retail and food manufacturing channels.
Higher tariffs on Canadian honey allow U.S. producers to capture demand from buyers seeking lower cost domestic supply.
U.S. importers pay a 50 percent tariff on Canadian clothing and fabric, which reduces orders as retail buyers avoid the higher landed cost.
U.S. importers pay the 50 percent tariff on Canadian makeup and perfumes, making these goods less attractive to U.S. retailers and consumers.
Canadian importers pay retaliatory tariffs on U.S. dairy, which raises the cost of U.S. dairy products in Canada and cuts export volume.
Retaliatory tariffs on U.S. dairy push Canadian buyers toward domestic dairy products, increasing sales for Canadian processors.
Canadian importers pay retaliatory tariffs on U.S. steel, making U.S. steel less competitive in Canadian industrial and construction markets.
Canadian buyers face higher costs for imported U.S. steel while Canadian steel producers gain share as buyers shift to domestic supply.
